questions.question: Define physical change and chemical change, give two examples of each, and state the single question that classifies any change.
questions.expected_answer: A physical change is a change in which no new substance forms: the particles themselves survive unchanged, and only their arrangement, spacing or energy changes, so the change is usually easy to reverse. Examples: chocolate melting in your pocket (still chocolate), Epsom salts dissolving in water (evaporation returns identical crystals), washing drying on the line, grating cheese. A chemical change is a change in which one or more new substances form with different properties: bonds break and new bonds form as the atoms regroup, so the change is usually difficult or impossible to reverse by simple means. Examples: a match burning (smoke, gases and a blackened stump), steel wool rusting to iron oxide, bread dough rising as yeast makes carbon dioxide, milk souring. The deciding question: is a new substance formed? Same substance afterwards — physical; new substance — chemical.

questions.question: List the five observable signs of a chemical change with an example of each, and use the fizzy-drink bubbles to explain why no single sign is proof on its own.
questions.expected_answer: One: a gas is produced — lemon juice on bicarbonate of soda foams with carbon dioxide; magnesium in dilute acid streams hydrogen. Two: a precipitate forms — two clear solutions meet and an insoluble yellow solid snows out. Three: a permanent colour change — a copper roof turning green, a cut avocado browning, steel wool rusting red-brown. Four: a temperature change nobody caused from outside — a hand warmer heating itself as iron combines with oxygen (exothermic), sherbet turning the tongue cold as it fizzes (endothermic). Five: light or sound from the change itself — a sparkler's white blaze, the pop of hydrogen meeting a flame. No single sign is proof because each can occur without chemistry: the bubbles rushing out of a just-opened fizzy drink look exactly like sign one, but that carbon dioxide was already dissolved in the liquid and is simply escaping — nothing new was made, so the change is physical. The signs raise suspicion; the verdict always rests on whether a new substance has actually formed.

questions.question: A burning candle shows both kinds of change at once, and burnt steel wool weighs more than the original metal. Explain both observations using the law of conservation of mass.
questions.expected_answer: At the top of the candle the flame's heat melts the wax — a physical change: a drop that runs down the side cools and hardens back into the same wax, so no new substance forms. At the wick the liquid wax burns — a chemical change: it combines with oxygen from the air to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, new substances that escape invisibly and can never be turned back into wax, which is why the candle grows permanently shorter. Neither change destroys atoms: weigh the candle before and after, capture all the gases, and count the oxygen the flame took from the air, and the totals balance exactly. Steel wool shows the same law from the other direction — the burnt ash weighs more than the metal because oxygen atoms from the air have joined the iron to form iron oxide; put that oxygen on the input side of the ledger and the mass of the products equals the mass of all the reactants. In every chemical change atoms are only regrouped, never created or destroyed.
